name: Definite/Indefinite Articles
explanation: When you describe a pain or symptom in a specific body part, Danish almost always uses the definite form of the noun (the "-en", "-et", or plural "-ene" ending), not the indefinite form. This is because you are referring to your own specific head, stomach, or back — not a head or a stomach in general. The pattern "ondt i + definite body part" is the standard way to say something hurts.

examples.english: I have a headache. (lit. I have pain in the head.)

examples.danish: Han har ondt i maven og ryggen.
examples.english: He has a stomach ache and a backache.

name: Present Perfect (førnutid)
explanation: To say how long you have had a symptom or how long you have been sick, Danish uses the present perfect ("har" + past participle) combined with a duration expression like "i tre dage" (for three days) or "siden i går" (since yesterday). This mirrors English "I have had..." but the construction and word order must be learned as a fixed pattern.

examples.danish: Jeg har haft feber i tre dage.
examples.english: I have had a fever for three days.

examples.danish: Hun har været syg siden i går.
examples.english: She has been sick since yesterday.

name: Modal Verbs (kan, skal, vil, må, bør)
explanation: In a healthcare context, modal verbs shift meaning slightly depending on how strong the advice is. "Skal" expresses a firm recommendation or instruction (you must/should), "bør" expresses a softer, more general recommendation (you ought to), and "må" expresses permission or a mild obligation. These are the same modal verbs from earlier modules, now used specifically to give or receive medical advice.

examples.danish: Du skal blive hjemme, hvis du har feber.
examples.english: You must stay home if you have a fever.

examples.danish: Du bør ringe til lægen og bestille en tid.
examples.english: You ought to call the doctor and book an appointment.
